newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Namibian chiefs lobby Europe against hydro scheme.
newsitem.headline: Namibian chiefs lobby Europe against hydro scheme.

text.p: Two Namibian tribal leaders are lobbying for support in Europe against a proposed $480 million hydroelectric scheme to be built on their ancestral land.
But the tour of chiefs Hikuminue Kapika and Paulus Tjavara to Germany, Sweden, Norway, Britain and the European Parliament in Belgium has drawn strong criticism from the Namibian government.

The chiefs have been at loggerheads with their government since the Epupa dam and hydro power scheme, planned for the Kunene River in northwestern Namibia, was put forward in 1991. They say the dam will destroy the ancestral graves and emergency grazing grounds of their nomadic Himba tribe.
The government has charged that the Himba chiefs are part of a "well-organised farce aimed at perpetuating European preconceptions and stereotypes about Africa".

"They are, through falsification and half truths, deliberately trying to mislead international public opinion on the facts relating to the Epupa project by replacing factual argument with farcical charades," said a statement by the Mines and Energy Ministry.

A parliamentarian for the Kunene region, Angelika Muharukua, also charged in parliament this week that the chiefs were not the true representatives of their people and had been bribed by whites who wanted to benefit from the Epupa Falls as a tourist attraction.
The government argues that the project provides the only feasible and cheap option to fulfil Namibia's future power needs and would bring development to the people of northwestern Namibia.

It has repeatedly dismissed concerns by environmental groups as attempts by Europeans to maintain the status quo of the Himba people as objects of curiosity being exhibited like zoo animals and denying them their right to development.

The chiefs' visit is being funded by a number of German environmental groups, including Arbeitskreis Afrika (Working Group Africa) and Gesellschaft fuer bedrohte Voelker (Society for Threatened Peoples).

A 23 million Namibian dollar ($5 million) environmental impact study funded by the Norwegian government and conducted by a consortium of Swedish, Norwegian, Namibian and Angolan consultants is due to be completed by October.
A final report will be submitted to the Namibian and Angolan governments for a decision in April 1998.
